standard.title: Content, structure and presentation separation
standard.description: represent documents online as content (text), structure (markup) and presentation (styling) and explain why such representations are important
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use a range of digital tools to create and communicate content (AC9TDI8P11, AC9TDI8P12). They have not yet formally encountered the three-layer model of web documents or the rationale for separating content, structure and presentation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent online documents by separating content (text), structure (HTML markup) and presentation (CSS styling), and explain why this separation is important for design, maintenance and accessibility.

nodes.label: The three layers of a web document
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and distinguish the three layers of an online document: content, structure and presentation.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a web page, identify what is content (text), what is structure (markup that organises the document), and what is presentation (how it looks).
nodes.typical_width: Describe what each layer contains and what role it plays; identify examples of HTML structural tags and CSS presentation rules in a web page.
wider: Compare how the same HTML document renders with and without CSS — articulate specifically what changed and what did not
Investigate how a screen reader interprets an HTML document and explain how structure (not presentation) determines what is communicated to the user

response_modes.reason: Distinguishing three layers is a precision task — students commonly assign CSS rules to 'structure' or treat HTML tags as presentation. Sufficient practice mapping specific examples (this text, this tag, this rule) to the correct layer builds the reliable discrimination needed before N2.

success_criteria: Correctly assigns specific examples (e.g. heading text, <h1> tag, font-size rule) to the correct layer
Does not confuse structural tags with visual appearance
nodes.hinge_reason: Misidentifying what belongs to content, structure, or presentation directly prevents N2 — students who conflate layers cannot correctly use HTML for structure and CSS for presentation.

nodes.label: Representing documents with HTML and CSS
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can write web pages using HTML for content and structure and CSS for styling, and explain how HTML tags separate content from structure.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a simple web page with at least two structural HTML elements and one CSS rule applied to them; explain what the tag does versus what the CSS rule does.
nodes.typical_width: Create a web page using HTML structural tags (headings, paragraphs, lists, divs) and CSS rules (colour, font, layout); explain how changing the CSS changes presentation without altering structure.
wider: Apply CSS classes to demonstrate how the same structural element can have different presentations in different contexts on the same page
Use CSS to implement a responsive layout that changes presentation based on screen width, explaining how presentation changes while structure remains constant

response_modes.reason: HTML/CSS syntax requires precision — misplaced tags, missing closing elements, and selector errors are common. Students need sufficient practice with the syntax to develop fluency before the conceptual significance of separation is legible to them.

success_criteria: HTML file uses structural tags correctly (headings, paragraphs, at minimum)
CSS rule targets an HTML element or class and changes its presentation
Student can explain what the HTML tag does versus what the CSS rule does
nodes.hinge_reason: Syntactic fluency at N2 is prerequisite for N3 — students who cannot produce working HTML/CSS cannot demonstrate the separation principle in action; they can only describe it abstractly, which does not meet the descriptor's demand.

nodes.label: Why separation matters
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why separating content, structure and presentation is important — specifically how it allows each to be designed, edited and stored independently.
nodes.minimum_width: Give at least one reason why separating content, structure and presentation is important — with a concrete example of the benefit.
nodes.typical_width: Explain multiple benefits of separation: independent editing, consistent presentation across many pages via a single CSS file, accessibility (structure legible to screen readers), and easier maintenance.
wider: Demonstrate the maintenance benefit by changing one CSS file to restyle an entire multi-page site, explaining why this would be impractical if styling were embedded in content
Investigate how major content management systems (e.g. WordPress themes) implement content/structure/presentation separation and explain the architectural choices
Examine how First Nations language preservation websites use structured content to support multiple language versions of the same page — explaining why structure separation makes this feasible

response_modes.reason: Students who have only produced a single small web page often struggle to appreciate why separation matters — the benefit is invisible at small scale. Multiple contexts (site-wide restyling, screen reader accessibility, multi-language content) each illuminate a different reason, making the principle concrete across scales.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The maintenance, accessibility and multilingual directions each make the separation principle concrete in a different way — rich for students who have grasped the mechanics and are ready to understand why the architecture exists.
success_criteria: Explains at least one concrete benefit of separation with a specific example
Connects the benefit to a real consequence (e.g. changing one CSS file updates many pages)
